title: Pentagon Awards Oracle $7 Billion Deal to Consolidate Military Software
excerpt: The enterprise-wide agreement, which could run up to 10 years, aims to eliminate fragmented software purchasing across the Defense Department and save taxpayers at least $441 million.
body:
• The Pentagon signed a nearly $7 billion, up-to-10-year agreement with Oracle to consolidate on-premises software licenses across the Defense Department, the Coast Guard, and the intelligence community.
  • The deal carries a base value of $3.31 billion over five years and is projected to save taxpayers at least $441 million by replacing fragmented, service-by-service contracts.
  • The contract follows a similar $9.69 billion consolidation deal with Microsoft signed in May, signaling a broad overhaul of how the military buys enterprise software.

Pentagon Strikes Sweeping Oracle Software Deal

The Pentagon on Thursday announced an enterprise-wide software agreement with Oracle worth up to $6.99 billion over 10 years, the second massive consolidation deal in three months as the department's technology chief pushes to eliminate years of duplicative spending across the military.

https://x.com/globeandmail/status/2080405541898318156

The Enterprise Software Agreement, negotiated by the Department of the Navy, covers Oracle's on-premises software, Software-as-a-Service applications, and professional services for the entire Defense Department, along with the U.S. Coast Guard and the intelligence community, according to Reuters.

The agreement has a base value of $3.31 billion over its initial five-year term. If the government exercises a five-year option, the total could reach $6.99 billion. The deal marks the Pentagon's first-ever direct contract with Oracle for its on-premises software use — previously, individual military branches maintained separate Oracle contracts, creating redundancy and inflated costs.

"By fundamentally improving how we procure on-premises Oracle capabilities, we are driving at least $441 million in taxpayer savings while rapidly and effectively serving our warfighters."

— Kirsten Davies, Pentagon Chief Information Officer

Part of a Broader Software Overhaul

The Oracle deal builds on a pattern set by Davies' office in May, when the Pentagon signed a five-year, $9.69 billion deal with Microsoft to consolidate enterprise software licenses scattered across the military services, the intelligence community, and the Coast Guard into a single contract.

Together, the two agreements represent a sweeping attempt to rein in what officials describe as years of fragmented procurement. Instead of dozens of service-level contracts with varying terms, the Pentagon is moving toward enterprise-wide frameworks that centralize purchasing and standardize technology across branches.

"Reducing fragmented procurement and advancing enterprise standardization will strengthen interoperability, reduce cybersecurity risk, and help us focus resources on resilient capabilities that can scale, integrate, and endure in contested conditions," said Barry Tanner, who is performing the duties of the Navy's chief information officer, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Oracle's Defense Push and the AI Factor

The indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract will allow Defense Department organizations to purchase Oracle commercial offerings through task and delivery orders tailored to specific mission requirements. Pricing, deliverables, and performance criteria will be defined at the order level.

Oracle has supplied technology to the Pentagon since the 1990s. The Austin-based company said military organizations will begin transitioning to the new contract framework this summer.

"For the Department of War, the challenge is not just finding the right technology, it's doing so quickly, compliantly, and at scale, without getting bogged down by complex procurement processes."

— Kim Lynch, Oracle Executive Vice President of Government, Defense and Intelligence

The deal arrives as the Defense Department accelerates its adoption of artificial intelligence and cloud computing. In January, the department unveiled an AI Acceleration Strategy aimed at speeding military AI deployment and reducing bureaucratic barriers. Oracle's cloud infrastructure has been positioning itself as a competitor to Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure in the government cloud market, particularly through its distributed cloud offerings that span 25-plus countries with FedRAMP High and classified-level authorizations.

Market Reaction and Political Context

Oracle shares rose roughly 2.5% in after-hours trading following the announcement, according to the Wall Street Journal. The stock has been a strong performer this year as the company benefits from surging demand for cloud infrastructure and AI services.

Reuters noted that Oracle founder and billionaire Larry Ellison maintains a close relationship with President Donald Trump. The political dimension adds a layer of scrutiny to large government contracts, though the deal was negotiated through standard procurement channels by the Navy.

What's Next

Military organizations are expected to begin transitioning to the new Oracle framework this summer. The contract's indefinite-delivery structure means the full scope and spending will depend on individual task orders placed by Defense Department agencies over the coming years.

The back-to-back Oracle and Microsoft deals suggest more enterprise-wide consolidations could follow as Davies' office continues its push to modernize the Pentagon's technology procurement. For Oracle, the contract deepens its footprint in a defense market increasingly shaped by cloud computing and AI — two areas where the company has been investing heavily to close the gap with larger rivals.
